title: Kitchen Know-How
summary: Short, useful pieces for every family cook: measurements and conversions, common substitutions, how to read a recipe, pantry staples and how long they keep, stocking a first kitchen on a budget, freezer tips, knife cuts and a glossary of cooking words.

table.note: Rounded metric values are NIST’s kitchen equivalents (1 tsp = 5 mL). A fluid ounce measures volume; an ounce on a scale measures weight. They match only for water and liquids like it.

list: A stick of butter is ½ cup, or 8 tablespoons.
Dry cups: scoop or spoon in and level off. Liquid cups: set on the counter and read at eye level.

links.d: Learn the kitchen chain teaspoon → gallon by heart.
The exact numbers behind every chart.

rows: 1 tablespoon vinegar or lemon juice plus enough milk to make 1 cup
¼ teaspoon baking soda plus ⅝ teaspoon cream of tartar
¾ cup honey, and use ¼ cup less liquid in the recipe
⅓ cup instant nonfat dry milk plus 1 cup minus 1 tablespoon water
table.note: From Utah State University Extension. Substitutions work best in cooking; in baking, expect small changes.

steps: Read it all the way through before you start, including the times. “Chill overnight” is easier to see before dinner than during.
Check the yield (how many it serves) and scale it if needed. The meal planner scales recipes for you.
Get everything out and measured first. Cooks call this *mise en place*, French for “everything in its place.”
Watch the order of words. “1 cup nuts, chopped” is measured, then chopped; “1 cup chopped nuts” is chopped, then measured.
Know the short forms: t or tsp = teaspoon; T or Tbsp = tablespoon; c = cup; oz = ounce; lb = pound; g = gram.
“Divided” means the ingredient is used in more than one step; “to taste” means add a little, taste, and adjust.
Preheat the oven when the recipe says, and use a thermometer for doneness, not the clock alone.

sections.h: Pantry staples and how long they keep

rows: Canned low-acid foods: beans, corn, peas, soups (not tomato), meat
Canned high-acid foods: tomatoes, fruit, pickles, citrus juice
table.note: From USDA. Store below 85°F, away from the stove and not under the sink. Throw out cans that bulge, leak, are heavily rusted, or have a deep dent, especially on a seam.

p: A starter pantry for family meals: rice, pasta, oats, flour, sugar, baking soda and powder, salt and pepper, a cooking oil, canned tomatoes, canned or dried beans, broth, peanut butter or another spread, and a few spices you use often (garlic powder, cinnamon, chili powder, Italian seasoning).

sections.h: Stocking a first kitchen on a budget
p: You don’t need a full set. These cover nearly every recipe on this site. Buy good basics once and add pieces as you find you need them; thrift stores and yard sales are good places for cast iron, glass dishes and bakeware.

list: Cast iron or stainless skillet (10 to 12 inch)
Wooden spoon, turner, tongs, rubber spatula, whisk
Mixing bowls and a few storage containers

links.d: What each tool is and how to care for it.

list: Cool food fast in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Label every container with what it is and the date.
Freeze soups and sauces flat in freezer bags with the air pressed out; they stack and thaw quickly.
Leave a little room at the top of rigid containers; food expands as it freezes.
Frozen food at 0°F stays safe; the freezer times on charts are for best quality, and leftovers taste best within 3 to 4 months.
Plan to eat refrigerated prep-day food within 3 to 4 days, or freeze it.

rows: Cut into small pieces; they don’t have to match.
Cut into small cubes, about ¼ inch on all sides.
Cut into tiny pieces, as for garlic.
Cut into thin strips, like matchsticks.
Cook uncovered in dry heat, usually in an oven.
Cook in dry oven heat; usually said of meat and vegetables.
Cook under direct heat from above.
Heat a liquid until bubbles rise and break all over the surface.
Cook in liquid just below boiling, with small bubbles rising slowly.
Cook slowly in a small amount of liquid in a covered pot.
Cook quickly in a little hot fat (from French *sauter*, “to jump”).
Cook small pieces quickly over high heat, stirring all the time.
Brown the outside quickly over high heat for flavor.
Cook on a rack or in a basket over a little boiling water, covered.
Boil a liquid to make less of it and concentrate its flavor.
Mix gently by cutting down through a mixture and turning it over, to keep air in.
Beat fat, like butter, with sugar until soft and smooth.
Press, fold and stretch dough until smooth.
Soak food in a flavored liquid.
